sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles introduced by Robert C. Martin (Uncle Bob). Following them makes software easier to maintain, extend, and test.

sections.heading: The Five Principles
items: S — Single Responsibility Principle: A class should have only one reason to change (one responsibility).
O — Open/Closed Principle: A class should be open for extension but closed for modification.
L — Liskov Substitution Principle: Subclasses should be substitutable for their parent class without breaking the program.
I — Interface Segregation Principle: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
D — Dependency Inversion Principle: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

sections.heading: Android Example
sections.content: Android's MVVM architecture naturally follows SOLID: ViewModel (SRP), Repository interface (OCP + DIP), LiveData/StateFlow (ISP — observe only what you need).

questions.question: What are different design patterns you know about?
questions.title: What are different design patterns you know about?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Design patterns are reusable solutions to recurring software design problems. The Gang of Four (GoF) book categorized 23 classic patterns into three groups.

sections.heading: Creational Patterns
items: Singleton — ensures only one instance of a class exists.
Factory Method — delegates object creation to subclasses.
Abstract Factory — creates families of related objects.
Builder — constructs complex objects step by step.
Prototype — clones existing objects.

sections.heading: Structural Patterns
items: Adapter — makes incompatible interfaces work together.
Decorator — adds behavior to objects dynamically.
Facade — provides a simplified interface to a subsystem.
Composite — treats individual objects and groups uniformly.
Proxy — controls access to another object.
Bridge — separates abstraction from implementation.
Flyweight — shares common state to reduce memory usage.

sections.heading: Behavioral Patterns
items: Observer — objects subscribe to and react to events.
Strategy — selects an algorithm at runtime.
Command — encapsulates a request as an object.
Template Method — defines a skeleton algorithm with steps overridden by subclasses.
Chain of Responsibility — passes a request along a chain of handlers.
State — changes behavior based on internal state.
Iterator — sequentially accesses elements of a collection.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Creational patterns deal with object creation mechanisms. They abstract the instantiation process, making a system independent of how its objects are created, composed, and represented.

sections.heading: Common Creational Patterns
items: Singleton — one instance globally (Application class in Android).
Factory Method — subclass decides which class to instantiate (ViewModelProvider.Factory).
Abstract Factory — creates families of related objects (Themed UI components).
Builder — step-by-step construction (AlertDialog.Builder, Retrofit.Builder).
Prototype — clone an existing object instead of creating from scratch.

sections.heading: Why It Matters
sections.content: Creational patterns provide flexibility in what gets created, who creates it, how it gets created, and when. They reduce tight coupling to specific classes.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Structural patterns deal with how classes and objects are composed to form larger structures. They simplify the design by identifying relationships between entities.

sections.heading: Common Structural Patterns
items: Adapter — wraps an incompatible interface (RecyclerView.Adapter bridges data and Views).
Decorator — adds responsibilities to objects dynamically (Kotlin extension functions, OkHttp interceptors).
Facade — hides complex subsystem behind a simple interface (Retrofit hides HTTP complexity).
Composite — tree structure of objects (Android View hierarchy).
Proxy — controls access to another object (Retrofit's dynamic proxy for API interfaces).
Bridge — decouples abstraction from implementation (separate platform rendering from logic).
Flyweight — shares state to minimize memory (Android's Bitmap Pool, String pool).

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Behavioral patterns are concerned with communication and responsibility between objects. They define how objects interact and distribute work.

sections.heading: Common Behavioral Patterns
items: Observer — LiveData, StateFlow, RxJava Observable in Android.
Strategy — pluggable sorting, caching, or authentication strategies.
Command — encapsulate operations as objects (undo/redo, WorkManager Tasks).
Template Method — Activity lifecycle (Android calls onCreate/onResume; you implement them).
Chain of Responsibility — OkHttp Interceptor chain.
State — manage UI states (Loading, Success, Error) via sealed classes.
Iterator — Kotlin's for-in loop over Iterable, Cursor in Room.

questions.question: Create Singleton Pattern without Kotlin default implementation
questions.title: Create Singleton Pattern without Kotlin default implementation

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Singleton ensures only one instance of a class exists across the application. In Kotlin, the object keyword provides it for free, but we can implement it manually for interview purposes.

sections.heading: Manual Singleton in Kotlin (Double-Checked Locking)
Key Points
items: @Volatile — ensures visibility of the instance variable across threads.
synchronized(this) — prevents two threads from creating instances simultaneously.
Double-check — first null check avoids unnecessary synchronization on every call.
Private constructor — prevents direct instantiation from outside.

questions.question: How to make a Singleton Pattern Thread Safe?
questions.title: How to make a Singleton Pattern Thread Safe?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: A basic null-check singleton is not thread-safe — two threads can both pass the null check simultaneously and create two instances. There are several approaches to fix this.

sections.heading: Approaches
items: 1. Synchronized method — simplest but slow; every call acquires a lock.
2. Double-Checked Locking — lock only on first creation; fast after initialization.
3. Eager initialization — create instance at class loading time; always thread-safe.
4. Kotlin object keyword — uses class loading guarantees; inherently thread-safe.
5. Initialization-on-demand holder — lazy + thread-safe via inner class loading.

sections.heading: Double-Checked Locking (Recommended)
Kotlin object (Best for Android)
Introduction
sections.content: The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency. When one object (Subject/Observable) changes state, all its dependents (Observers) are notified and updated automatically.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: LiveData (observers = UI), StateFlow (collect = observe), RxJava Observable, BroadcastReceiver, View.OnClickListener — all follow Observer pattern.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Adapter pattern converts the interface of a class into another interface that clients expect. It lets classes work together that couldn't otherwise due to incompatible interfaces — like a power plug adapter.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Example
sections.content: RecyclerView.Adapter adapts a List<Item> data source to the View items the RecyclerView framework expects. You provide the adapter; the framework calls onCreateViewHolder() and onBindViewHolder().

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) states two things: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules — both should depend on abstractions. And abstractions should not depend on details — details should depend on abstractions.

sections.heading: Violation — High-level depends on Low-level
Following DIP — Both depend on abstraction
Benefits
items: Testable — inject a FakeUserRepository in unit tests.
Flexible — swap implementations without changing the ViewModel.
Foundation for Dependency Injection frameworks like Hilt/Dagger.

questions.question: Write a real-life example of Dependency Injection without using any library
questions.title: Write a real-life example of Dependency Injection without using any library

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Dependency Injection (DI) is a technique where an object's dependencies are provided from outside rather than created inside. This makes code testable, flexible, and loosely coupled.

sections.heading: Manual DI — Constructor Injection
Types of DI
items: Constructor Injection — dependencies passed via constructor (preferred).
Setter Injection — dependencies set via property or setter method.
Interface Injection — dependency provides an injector method the dependent implements.

questions.question: Explain how Android Architecture components utilize design patterns behind the scenes
questions.title: Explain how Android Architecture components utilize design patterns behind the scenes

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Android Architecture Components (ViewModel, LiveData, Room, WorkManager) are all built on well-known design patterns. Understanding them helps you use these components more effectively.

sections.heading: ViewModel
items: Factory Pattern — ViewModelProvider.Factory creates the ViewModel; you define how it's constructed.
Facade Pattern — ViewModel exposes a clean interface for the UI while hiding repository/data-fetch complexity.
MVVM Pattern — ViewModel is literally the 'VM' in MVVM, separating UI state from View.

sections.heading: LiveData
items: Observer Pattern — Activity/Fragment observes LiveData and reacts to changes.
Null Object Pattern — LiveData.value is null by default; prevents NullPointerException at registration.
Lifecycle awareness — built-in State pattern that only notifies active observers.

sections.heading: Room
items: Repository Pattern — DAOs abstract the SQL details; the app code never writes raw SQL.
Proxy Pattern — Room generates DAO implementations at compile time via annotation processing.
Builder Pattern — Room.databaseBuilder() constructs the database step by step.

sections.heading: WorkManager
items: Command Pattern — each Worker encapsulates a unit of work to be scheduled and executed.
Chain of Responsibility — WorkManager.beginWith().then() chains workers.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Builder pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. It lets you create an object step by step with a fluent API, and only produces the final object when build() is called.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: AlertDialog.Builder, Retrofit.Builder, OkHttpClient.Builder, NotificationCompat.Builder, Room.databaseBuilder() — all use this pattern.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Factory pattern defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate. It decouples object creation from object usage.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Example
sections.content: ViewModelProvider.Factory creates ViewModel instances. Hilt generates factories automatically. Fragment.instantiate() is an Android framework factory method.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Repository pattern mediates between the domain and data layers using a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects. It abstracts whether data comes from a network, database, or cache.

sections.heading: Implementation
Benefits
items: Single source of truth — all data access goes through one place.
Testable — inject FakeRepository in ViewModel tests.
Swappable — change from REST to GraphQL without touching ViewModel.
Caching logic centralized — not scattered across the app.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Facade pattern provides a simplified, unified interface to a complex subsystem. It hides the complexity of multiple classes behind a single class.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: Retrofit is a facade over OkHttp + Gson/Moshi + threading. Glide is a facade over bitmap decoding + caching + threading. Context is a facade over Android system services.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable at runtime. The client code doesn't know which algorithm runs — it just calls the strategy.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: Glide's DiskCacheStrategy enum, OkHttp's CacheControl, Collections.sort() with different Comparators, RecyclerView's ItemAnimator — all implement Strategy pattern.

questions.question: What design patterns are used in Retrofit library source code?
questions.title: What design patterns are used in Retrofit library source code?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Retrofit is one of the most pattern-rich libraries in the Android ecosystem. Understanding its internals reveals how expert-level library design works.

sections.heading: Patterns Used in Retrofit
items: Builder Pattern — Retrofit.Builder() constructs the Retrofit instance step by step with baseUrl, converter factories, and call adapter factories.
Facade Pattern — Retrofit hides OkHttp, Gson/Moshi, and threading complexity behind a simple annotated interface.
Proxy Pattern — Retrofit.create(ApiService::class.java) returns a dynamic proxy (Java's Proxy.newProxyInstance). Every method call on the API interface is intercepted and converted to an OkHttp call.
Factory Pattern — CallAdapter.Factory and Converter.Factory decide how to convert responses (Gson, Moshi, Kotlin serialization) and how to return them (Call, Observable, suspend).
Adapter Pattern — CallAdapter adapts OkHttp's Call to Kotlin suspend functions, RxJava Observables, etc.
Template Method — ServiceMethod defines the template for processing an API call; subclasses (HttpServiceMethod) handle specifics.

questions.question: What design patterns are used in Glide image loading library?
questions.title: What design patterns are used in Glide image loading library?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Glide is a complex image loading pipeline with multiple design patterns working together to provide efficient, flexible image loading.

sections.heading: Patterns Used in Glide
items: Builder Pattern — Glide.with(context).load(url).placeholder().error().into(imageView) is a fluent builder chain.
Strategy Pattern — DiskCacheStrategy (NONE, DATA, RESOURCE, ALL, AUTOMATIC) switches caching behavior at runtime.
Factory Pattern — ModelLoaderFactory and DataFetcherFactory create the appropriate loaders for different input types (URL, File, URI, resource).
Flyweight Pattern — Glide reuses Bitmap objects via BitmapPool instead of creating new ones — reduces GC pressure.
Decorator Pattern — Transformations (CenterCrop, CircleCrop, RoundedCorners) wrap and modify bitmaps without altering the loader chain.
Observer Pattern — Target (ImageViewTarget, CustomTarget) observes the loading lifecycle (onResourceReady, onLoadFailed).
Lifecycle awareness — Glide attaches a headless Fragment to the Activity/Fragment to observe lifecycle events (pause/resume/destroy requests).

questions.question: What are examples of Observer pattern used in Android?
questions.title: What are examples of Observer pattern used in Android?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Observer pattern is the most pervasive design pattern in Android. The entire reactive programming model in Android is built on it.

sections.heading: Observer Pattern in Android
items: LiveData — Activity/Fragment observes LiveData; auto-unsubscribes on lifecycle destroy.
StateFlow / SharedFlow — coroutine-based observers using collect {} block.
RxJava Observable — classic reactive pattern; subscribe() registers observers.
BroadcastReceiver — registers to receive system or custom broadcast events.
View.OnClickListener — button.setOnClickListener{} observes click events.
ContentObserver — observes changes to ContentProvider data (contacts, media).
SensorEventListener — observes accelerometer, gyroscope sensor changes.
RecyclerView.AdapterDataObserver — RecyclerView observes adapter for data changes.
Jetpack Compose — State<T> and MutableState cause recomposition (implicit observer).

questions.question: What design patterns are used in AOSP (Android Open Source Project)?
questions.title: What design patterns are used in AOSP (Android Open Source Project)?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: AOSP itself is a masterclass in design patterns. The Android framework was designed by engineers applying GoF patterns to build a flexible, extensible mobile platform.

sections.heading: Patterns in AOSP
items: Singleton — Application class, ActivityManagerService, PackageManagerService — system services are singletons.
Observer — BroadcastReceiver, ContentObserver, SensorEventListener, Handler/Looper message queue.
Factory — Fragment.instantiate(), LayoutInflater (creates View objects from XML), ViewModelProvider.Factory.
Adapter — RecyclerView.Adapter, CursorAdapter, ArrayAdapter — all bridge data to View.
Template Method — Activity lifecycle (the framework calls onCreate/onStart/onResume; subclasses override).
Composite — Android View hierarchy: ViewGroup contains Views; treated uniformly via draw(), measure(), layout().
Proxy — Binder IPC (inter-process communication) creates proxies for system services across processes.
Command — Pending Intent (encapsulates an Intent to be fired later by another app or alarm).
Decorator — Context → ContextWrapper → ContextThemeWrapper adds decoration layers over base Context.
Chain of Responsibility — Touch event dispatch chain (Activity → ViewGroup → View).
Flyweight — Android's String pool, Bitmap recycle pool, Message.obtain() from message pool.
State — Activity/Fragment lifecycle managed as a state machine (CREATED, STARTED, RESUMED, etc.).

questions.question: Kotlin Optional Parameters vs Builder Pattern — when to use which?
questions.title: Kotlin Optional Parameters vs Builder Pattern — when to use which?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Kotlin's default/named parameters solve many of the same problems that the Builder pattern was invented to solve in Java. Knowing when to prefer each is an important Kotlin design decision.

sections.heading: Kotlin Optional Parameters
items: Concise — no extra Builder class needed.
Type-safe — compiler enforces required vs optional parameters.
Best for: data classes, simple configuration objects, internal Kotlin-only APIs.
Example: data class Config(val host: String, val port: Int = 8080, val timeout: Int = 30)

sections.heading: Builder Pattern
items: Java interoperability — Kotlin default params don't work cleanly from Java code.
Validation at build time — Builder can validate combinations before constructing.
Complex construction — steps have side effects, ordering matters, or creation is async.
Public API / SDK — @JvmOverloads partially helps, but Builder is cleaner for Java consumers.
Example: Retrofit.Builder, OkHttpClient.Builder.

sections.heading: Rule of Thumb
sections.content: For Kotlin-only internal code: use default parameters. For public APIs consumed from Java or complex validated construction: use Builder. Use @JvmOverloads as a middle ground.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality by wrapping objects in decorator classes.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: OkHttp Interceptors (each interceptor decorates the next), Context → ContextWrapper → ContextThemeWrapper, Kotlin extension functions (syntactic decorator), Jetpack Compose Modifier chain.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Command pattern encapsulates a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undoable operations.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: PendingIntent encapsulates an Intent command to be fired later. WorkManager Workers encapsulate background tasks. Menu items with setOnMenuItemClickListener — each item is a command.

questions.question: What is the Template Method Pattern?
questions.title: What is the Template Method Pattern?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, deferring some steps to subclasses. Subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall algorithm structure.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: Activity lifecycle is the most famous Android example — the framework calls onCreate → onStart → onResume in sequence; you override the steps. AsyncTask (deprecated) used the same pattern: doInBackground + onPostExecute.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Prototype pattern creates new objects by copying (cloning) an existing object — the prototype. It is useful when object creation is expensive and a similar object already exists.

sections.heading: Implementation in Kotlin
When to Use
items: Object construction is expensive (database reads, network calls).
You need many similar objects with minor differences.
Kotlin data class copy() is effectively a built-in Prototype implementation.
Android example: creating multiple similar notification configurations from a base template.

questions.question: What is the Chain of Responsibility Pattern?
questions.title: What is the Chain of Responsibility Pattern?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Chain of Responsibility pattern passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides to process the request or pass it to the next handler in the chain.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: OkHttp Interceptor chain (each interceptor calls chain.proceed()), Android touch event dispatch (Activity → ViewGroup → View), exception handling chains.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The State pattern allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class. It replaces complex if-else or when chains based on state.

sections.heading: Implementation with Sealed Class
Android Examples
sections.content: Sealed class UiState (Loading/Success/Error), Activity lifecycle state machine, MediaPlayer states (idle, prepared, playing, paused), Bluetooth connection states.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Proxy pattern provides a surrogate or placeholder object that controls access to another object. It adds a layer of indirection for access control, lazy initialization, logging, or caching.

sections.heading: Types of Proxies
items: Virtual Proxy — delays expensive object creation until first use (lazy initialization).
Protection Proxy — controls access based on permissions.
Remote Proxy — represents an object in a different address space (Binder in Android).
Caching Proxy — stores results of expensive operations.

sections.heading: Lazy Virtual Proxy in Kotlin
Android Examples
sections.content: Retrofit.create() returns a dynamic Java Proxy. Android Binder IPC is a remote proxy. Kotlin's lazy {} delegate is a virtual proxy. Room's generated DAO implementations are compile-time proxies.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Composite pattern composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly through a common interface.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: The Android View hierarchy is the canonical Composite pattern: ViewGroup (Folder) contains View children. draw(), measure(), and layout() are called recursively on the tree.

questions.question: What is the Abstract Factory Pattern?
questions.title: What is the Abstract Factory Pattern?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. It's a factory of factories.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Example
sections.content: Material Design component theming — a theme factory creates consistent Button, TextField, Card styles across the app. Hilt's component hierarchy provides related object graphs (ApplicationComponent → ActivityComponent).

questions.question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
questions.title: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: A class should have only one reason to change. This means each class should have a single, well-defined responsibility — one job, one concern.

sections.heading: Violation
Correct SRP
Benefits
items: Easier to test each class in isolation.
Changes to one responsibility don't affect others.
Classes are smaller, more readable, and focused.
The Android MVVM architecture enforces SRP by design.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Software entities (classes, modules, functions) should be open for extension but closed for modification. You add new behavior by adding new code, not by changing existing tested code.

sections.heading: Violation
Following OCP

questions.question: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?
questions.title: What is the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)?

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without breaking the application. Subclasses must honour the contract of the base class — they can extend it but never weaken it.

sections.heading: Violation — Classic Rectangle/Square Problem
LSP Fix
items: Don't extend Square from Rectangle — they have different contracts.
Use a common Shape interface instead.
Android example: any subclass of RecyclerView.Adapter must correctly implement getItemCount(), onBindViewHolder() — breaking this contract crashes the RecyclerView.

questions.question: What is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
questions.title: What is the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?

sections.heading: Definition
sections.content: Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they don't use. Instead of one large interface, create several small, specific interfaces so clients only implement what they need.

sections.heading: Violation
Following ISP

questions.question: What is the MVI (Model-View-Intent) architecture pattern?
questions.title: What is the MVI (Model-View-Intent) architecture pattern?

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: MVI is a unidirectional data flow architecture pattern commonly used with Jetpack Compose. It treats user actions as Intents, processes them into a State, and renders the State. Unlike MVVM, state flows in one direction only.

sections.heading: Components
items: Model (State) — immutable data class representing the complete UI state at any moment.
View — renders the current State; sends user Intents to the ViewModel.
Intent — sealed class representing user actions or events (not Android Intent).

sections.heading: Implementation
MVI vs MVVM
items: MVI has a single immutable state — no risk of multiple LiveData values being out of sync.
Unidirectional data flow — easier to reason about, test, and debug.
Better for Compose — Compose is designed around state rendering.
More boilerplate — each screen needs Intent, State, and ViewModel wired together.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The Flyweight pattern reduces memory usage by sharing common state between many fine-grained objects. Instead of storing all data per object, it separates intrinsic (shared) state from extrinsic (unique) state.

sections.heading: Implementation
Android Examples
sections.content: RecyclerView's ViewHolder pool (reuses views), Android's BitmapPool in Glide (reuses Bitmap memory), Java String pool, Message.obtain() pool, Drawable caches in Resources.
